response.query: How will we sample finite‑temperature effects (harmonic approximations, anharmonic corrections, ab initio MD) and decide between periodic slab versus cluster support models with quantitative benchmarks?
response.answer: Finite-temperature effects are sampled using harmonic approximations, anharmonic corrections, and ab initio molecular dynamics. Periodic slab models are preferred for extended systems, while cluster models are used for localized systems, with benchmarks based on accuracy and computational cost.

results.title: Anharmonic effects in the quantum cluster equilibrium method | The Journal of Chemical Physics | AIP Publishing
results.content: Research Article| March 27 2017. # Anharmonic effects in the quantum cluster equilibrium method *Available to Purchase*. Search for other works by this author on:. Search for other works by this author on:. * *Views Icon* Views *Open Menu*. Michael von Domaros, Eva Perlt; Anharmonic effects in the quantum cluster equilibrium method. The well-established quantum cluster equilibrium (QCE) model provides a statistical thermodynamic framework to apply high-level *ab initio* calculations of finite cluster structures to macroscopic liquid phases using the partition function. In this article, we apply an important correction in the evaluation of the one-particle partition function and account for anharmonicity. Therefore, we implemented an analytical approximation to the Morse partition function and the derivatives of its logarithm with respect to temperature, which are required for the evaluation of thermodynamic quantities. This anharmonic QCE approach has been applied to liquid hydrogen chloride and cluster distributions, and the molar volume, the volumetric thermal expansion coefficient, and the isobaric heat capacity have been calculated. An improved description for all properties is observed if anharmonic effects are considered. results.title: Piezoelectric coefficients by molecular dynamics simulations in the constant stress ensemble: A case study of quartz - ScienceDirect
results.content: # Piezoelectric coefficients by molecular dynamics simulations in the constant stress ensemble: A case study of quartz. Piezoelectric (strain) coefficients of quartz are calculated in terms of molecular dynamics as a function of pressure and temperature. We review the necessary formulas for the computation of electromechanical materials coefficients obtained at constant stress and temperature, and discuss how to overcome complications of the definition of polarization variations due to fluctuating box geometries. As we will outline further below, the ambiguity in defining the polarization becomes particularly delicate, even in classical molecular dynamics simulations, when one treats a system containing free charges at finite temperature and constant stress, which implies fluctuating box shapes. The problem of defining the proper polarization for periodically repeated cells arises in force-field and ab-initio calculations. While a lot of work has been published on the calculation of the proper polarization in ab-initio calculations [2], [3], [4], [5] much less attention has been paid to thermo-mechanical and dielectric properties obtained from calculations that are based on force fields. While such methods have been sketched in the literature, often in terms of harmonic approximations neglecting anharmonic fluctuation corrections [6], we are unaware of literature, in which (various) ways are stated explicitly how to calculate dielectric and piezoelectric susceptibility tensor in molecular dynamics or Monte Carlo simulations. The suggested ways to calculate electromechanical properties promise to be beneficial for the future, if *reliable*, transferable potentials become available so that complex structures can be studied that are not amenable to *ab-initio* simulations. In order to provide expressions for the calculation of electromechanical coefficients at finite temperatures, we discuss the free energy of a dielectric as a function of bulk polarization and strain as well as of the geometry of the periodically repeated (simulation) cell. In this paper, we discussed various methods to compute the piezoelectric response within the framework of molecular dynamics simulations that are based on classical force fields and that employ effective charges as well as (inducible) dipoles. A classical molecular dynamics model with an incorporated strain-dependent dipole potential energy term is introduced to represent the piezoelectric properties of boron nitride nanotubes (BNNTs).
